documents: Gilbert, Orr, Renfrew, King & Lachlan-Cope (2022), A 20-year study of melt processes over Larsen C ice shelf using a high-resolution regional atmospheric model: 2. Drivers of surface melting, JGR Atmospheres 127, e2021JD036012 (published PDF, 19 pages)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (article pages printed as 'n of 19')

entry.evidence: To date, no work has attempted to assess the relative importance of the first-order drivers of surface melting on Larsen C

sequences.source_document: Gilbert et al. 2022, JGR Atmospheres 127, e2021JD036012 (published PDF)

steps.action: Assembled from the literature the candidate drivers of Larsen C surface melt: solar radiation, foehn winds, cloud phase and cover, and large-scale circulation (SAM, ENSO, ASL, barrier winds).
steps.quote: Foehn winds cause leeside warming and associated melting over these ice shelves

steps.action: Identified the gap that no multidecadal study ranks these drivers, and set the aim of quantifying their relative importance over a multidecadal period.
steps.quote: the aim of this investigation is to robustly quantify the importance of the various drivers of Larsen C surface melting over a multidecadal period

steps.action: Used the 4 km MetUM hindcast (1998–2017, ERA-Interim boundaries) built and validated against AWS data in Part 1, noting its warm, windy and moist biases and underestimated Emelt.
steps.quote: examining output from the high-resolution multidecadal MetUM hindcast of the Antarctic Peninsula described in Part 1 of this study

steps.action: Designed the analysis: diagnosed each condition from model indicator variables or observed indices with set thresholds (Table 1; isentrope-based foehn detection from Part 1), then composited SEB and melt and computed Pearson correlations, seasonally.
steps.quote: The relative importance of various drivers of surface melting is assessed by examining periods when certain conditions prevail

steps.action: Composited high-melt periods (>75th percentile) and found north-westerly cross-peninsula flow in all seasons, with nonsummer melt concentrated in a few intense events.
steps.quote: Figure 2 shows that for all seasons, instances of high melting over Larsen C occur during periods of north-westerly flow

steps.action: Compared melt share against frequency of occurrence for sunny conditions, with correlations of Emelt against SEB terms (Tables 2 and 3, Figure 3), and found SW radiation the leading driver.
steps.quote: these results suggest that SW radiation is the most important driver of surface melting on Larsen C overall

steps.action: Compared melt share against frequency for foehn conditions by season and found foehn second overall but dominant in MAM.
steps.quote: foehn events are an important driver of surface melting over the Larsen C ice shelf year-round but are especially important in nonsummer seasons

steps.action: Checked the foehn result with a second method, correlating Emelt with sensible and latent heat fluxes as foehn proxies, and judged the support weak but consistent.
steps.quote: cannot conclusively demonstrate the importance of foehn in driving surface melting. However, they add weight to the evidence presented above.

steps.action: Separated SW and foehn effects by compositing sunny foehn, nonsunny foehn and sunny nonfoehn conditions (Figure 4), showing season-dependent dominance.
steps.quote: allows us to further elucidate the relative importance of SW and foehn on melting over Larsen [...]

steps.action: Compared melt share against frequency for cloudy conditions and found cloud suppresses melt in DJF and SON but enhances it in MAM and JJA through increased LW↓.
steps.quote: despite occurring 62% of the time in DJF, “cloudy” conditions are associated with just 50% of melt

steps.action: Checked the cloud result against an alternative definition (high LWP > 75th percentile) and found the composites virtually identical.
steps.quote: synoptic conditions and SEB anomalies during “cloudy” conditions are virtually indistinguishable from those during the “high LWP” regime

steps.action: Tested foehn-induced cloud clearance using co-occurrences of foehn with sunny, clear and low-LWP conditions (Table 4, Table S1, Figure 5) and found it rare but associated with high melt when it occurs.
steps.quote: implying that foehn-induced cloud clearance may drive above-average summertime melt when it occurs, but that such conditions occur fairly infrequently

steps.action: Composited SAM±, ENSO±, ASL and barrier-wind conditions (Table 2, Figure 6) and found that SAM+, ENSO− and deep ASL enhance melt through their effect on flow, foehn and the SEB.
steps.quote: Table 2 suggests that SAM+ and ENSO− enhance surface melting in DJF and MAM

steps.action: Correlated modeled seasonal and annual foehn frequency with the observed SAM index across 20 years (Table 5, Figure 7); the correlation is significant except in JJA.
steps.quote: The correlation between annually averaged SAM index and annual mean foehn frequency is 0.52 in inlets and 0.54 at over the ice shelf

steps.action: Composited melt-suppressing conditions (barrier winds, SAM−, ENSO+) and attributed suppression mainly to cold temperature anomalies.
steps.quote: Barrier wind conditions are associated with extremely negative Tmax and Emelt anomalies across the entire Larsen C ice shelf

steps.action: Kept the ranking of drivers: SW radiation first, then foehn, then cloud, then large-scale circulation, with interactions among them noted.
steps.quote: this study has systematically ranked the conditions that drive surface melt in order of importance

Partly; joint conditioning, an alternative cloud definition and flux-proxy correlations; no threshold sensitivity tests
Ranking kept: SW > foehn > cloud > large-scale circulation

end.claim: In the 1998–2017 MetUM hindcast, solar radiation is the primary driver of Larsen C surface melt, followed by foehn (dominant in nonsummer seasons), then cloud, then large-scale circulation (SAM, ENSO, ASL), which acts through the other drivers.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the share of meltwater produced under each diagnosed condition against how often that condition occurs (Table 2) is what turns the composites into a ranking.

gates.evidence: The conditions to composite were chosen from drivers named in the literature (p. 4), but the hindcast was produced in Part 1 for general melt studies, not to test these drivers. The ranking could have come out differently, but it was not tested against observations or against a stated failure criterion (pp. 6–16). Some thresholds were taken from external conventions fixed beforehand (Kay et al. 2008 cloud fractions; the NOAA ±0.5 °C ENSO rule; p. 5); others (percentiles, 5 m s−1 barrier wind) were chosen by the authors, with no statement that they were fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Pearson correlation coefficients with two-sided p values

novelty_claims.quote: We evaluate the contribution of various atmospheric conditions in order to identify and rank, for the first time, the most significant causes of melting
To date, no work has attempted to assess the relative importance of the first-order drivers of surface melting on Larsen C
the importance of cloud-mediated melting on Larsen C has not been examined over multiple decades
its significance has not yet been established across larger spatial and temporal scales on Larsen C

limits: No review file was supplied; the acknowledgments mention two reviewers of an earlier version, but no review sequence can be coded. The whole result rests on one model hindcast. Its known biases (Emelt and Rnet underestimated, more so at inlets and in DJF, p. 4) are not propagated into the melt shares. The ranking is not checked against observations. Composite thresholds (percentiles, 5 m s−1 barrier wind, ±1σ SAM, foehn detection rule) are not varied. Conditions overlap, so melt shares sum to more than 100% and attribution is not exclusive. Sub-claims at other statuses: the SAM–foehn relation is regularity_in_range (1998–2017; r = 0.46–0.66 in DJF, MAM and SON, insignificant in JJA; p. 15). Foehn-induced cloud clearance is left without a conclusion ('further investigation is required', p. 12). The claims that cloud-mediated melt and SAM-driven foehn will matter more in a warming climate are projections inferred from cited studies, not tested here (pp. 11, 16). Inconsistencies noted by the coder: the Summary gives r = 0.62 as the SAM–foehn correlation (p. 16), which is the DJF ice-shelf value, while the annual values are 0.52 and 0.54 (Table 5). The LW↓ correlations on p. 11 are attributed to Table 2 but appear in Table 3. Composition: coded natures_repetition because conditions are found, not set, and repeated across 20 model years; the fit is imperfect, since the headline claim is a ranking of overlapping drivers rather than a fitted regularity, and the model could in principle have been used to remove drivers (sensitivity runs) but was not (inference).

disagreements.target: van Wessem et al. (2015, 2016), RACMO2.3 at 5.5 km
disagreements.support: The paper argues that a hydrostatic model at 5.5 km cannot resolve the steep topography needed for foehn, while noting that later work found RACMO2.3 satisfactory for foehn.
disagreements.quote: its hydrostatic core prohibits the use of kilometer scale spatial resolution

disagreements.target: Bozkurt et al. (2020), WRF hindcast at 15 km
disagreements.support: The paper argues that the resolution is too coarse to resolve foehn, which motivates the 4 km MetUM hindcast.
disagreements.quote: insufficiently fine-scale to adequately resolve important features such as foehn winds

disagreements.target: Short-period process studies (King et al. 2015; Gilbert et al. 2020; Elvidge et al. 2020)
disagreements.support: These studies cover one to six months; the paper extends the analysis to a 20-year hindcast.
disagreements.quote: but this process-focused study is limited in its duration to 6 months

disagreements.target: Foehn clearance as an explanation of enhanced melt (Kuipers Munneke et al. 2012; Grosvenor et al. 2014; Cape et al. [...]
disagreements.support: Co-occurrence statistics (Table 4, Table S1) show that clearance events are rare, and that foehn mostly enhances melt during conditions that are already sunny.
disagreements.quote: Foehn-induced cloud clearance may drive large Emelt anomalies but this occurs relatively infrequently in the hindcast

alternatives_considered.alternatives: RACMO2.3 at 5.5 km; WRF at 15 km; MAR at 7.5 km
alternatives_considered.reason: Kilometre-scale resolution is needed to resolve steep topography and foehn
Liquid cloud was shown to exert a more important control on the SEB and melt in Gilbert et al. (2020)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Composites for SON, DJF and MAM only
alternatives_considered.reason: Very little SW↓ in JJA and <0.1% of meltwater production
The two are virtually indistinguishable, so figures were omitted to avoid repetition

alternatives_considered.chosen: Foehn clearance defined by combining clear, sunny and low-LWP criteria with foehn
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Coincidence of clear and foehn periods based on cloud fraction alone
alternatives_considered.reason: Model cloud fraction is parameterized and less reliable than LWP or solar radiation

alternatives_considered.chosen: Circulation composites shown for DJF only
alternatives_considered.reason: The absolute influence on Emelt is strongest in DJF
